oneliner.t: Republican U.S. Representative for Iowa's 2nd District since 2021 and former KCRG-TV journalist who won the June 2, 2026 GOP primary for Iowa's open U.S. Senate seat (Joni Ernst retiring), with Trump's endorsement.

hometown.t: West Des Moines area (graduated Valley High School, West Des Moines)

upbringing.t: Born in Des Moines and a graduate of Valley High School in West Des Moines; she left Iowa for college in Los Angeles, earning a broadcast journalism degree at USC, where she interned at KABC-TV. She came back to Iowa for TV news and spent more than a decade at KCRG-TV in Cedar Rapids. Her official bio says she reported on health-care costs and flooding and is a two-time regional Emmy winner. She married Matt Arenholz, an insurance executive, in 2008, and they are raising two sons in Marion. Her parents and early family life are not described in the sources reviewed.

education.school: Valley High School, West Des Moines

career.yrs: more than a decade, ending about 2016 (exact years not documented)

platform.t: Pledged at launch to be President Trump's 'strongest ally' in the Senate and deliver the America First agenda; in the Oct. 7 debate she said she would be his ally when it benefits Iowa and push back when needed.
Tighter border security and deporting people in the country illegally; supports continuing border-wall construction (2021).

Blocking regulations she says burden farmers, expanding biofuels (E15); introduced the EATS Act (2023) to block state production standards such as California's Prop 12; criticized Trump's temporary lifting of beef-import tariffs (Aug. 2026).

Says she will protect Medicaid, Medicare and Social Security; wants a bipartisan commission on Social Security solvency and is open to gradually raising the retirement age; did not back lifting the payroll-tax cap.

Says the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act lowered costs and protects Medicaid for those most in need while removing people 'gaming the system'; voted against a three-year extension of ACA subsidies in January 2026.
Voted against Iran war-powers resolutions, including in September 2026, but on Sept. 21, 2026 called for an immediate end to the war and later for pausing diesel exports and suspending the gas tax.
Tax cuts, family tax credits, help for expectant mothers and midwife access, and child-care affordability.
Promotes a proposal to bar members of Congress from trading individual stocks.
Opposes transgender girls in girls' sports; rated pro-life; voted for the Respect for Marriage Act in 2022.
Wants a stronger military and a harder line on China (supply chains, trade penalties); sits on the House Select Committee on the CCP.

promises.t: Be President Trump's 'strongest ally' in the Senate.
Protect Medicaid, Medicare and Social Security; set up a bipartisan commission on Social Security solvency.
Secure the border and deport people in the country illegally.
Expand biofuels and block regulations she says burden farmers.
Bar members of Congress from trading individual stocks.

claims.claim: Reported for KCRG-TV in Cedar Rapids for more than a decade and is a two-time Midwest regional Emmy winner.

said.where: official House bio (hinson.house.gov/about); her Senate campaign site could not be opened

record.t: Wikipedia confirms she anchored at KCRG-TV but gives no years; no independent record of the awards was found.

claims.claim: Served in the Iowa House representing District 67.

record.t: Represented District 67 from Jan. 9, 2017 to Jan. 3, 2021; won in 2016 (62.5%) and 2018 (52%).

claims.claim: Worked across the aisle on child-care access and federal lobbying bans.

said.where: campaign website as quoted by Ballotpedia News

record.t: Neither source names bill numbers, cosponsors or outcomes, so the claim could not be checked against congress.gov in this pass.

claims.claim: 'We decided to sell our individual stocks right away in 2021.'

record.t: The House Clerk index shows one periodic transaction report filed April 5, 2021, consistent with 2021 trades, but the report itself was not opened. A Democratic-party summary of an Iowa Independent review says she disclosed buying and selling stocks in 2021. Separately, her 2025 disclosure lists her husband's $1M–$5M interest in a private insurance brokerage (not a publicly traded stock).

claims.claim: Her family's wealth grew because her husband sold his insurance business in 2021.

record.t: NOTUS reports her 2021 disclosure shows her husband sold an interest in a private insurance company for over $1 million. Her 2025 disclosure also lists his $1M–$5M stake in High Street Insurance Partners, which the ethics complaint says paid up to $1M in 2025 dividends, so the 2021 sale is not the only source of the growth.

claims.claim: 'Josh Turek skipped 58% of the votes at the State House this year.'

said.where: X post (early September), repeated in Oct. 7 debate

record.t: PolitiFact found Turek missed 261 of 445 votes (58%) in the 2026 session; he missed 9.8% in 2025 and has about 81% attendance since 2023.

claims.claim: First Senate TV ad (May 12, 2026): she is lowering health-insurance costs, supporting veterans and banning congressional stock trading.

said.where: first statewide TV ad, as described by the Iowa Democratic Party

record.t: Iowa Capital Dispatch confirms she voted in January 2026 against a three-year extension of ACA subsidies. The Iowa Independent review (via a partisan release) says she had not signed a 2025 stock-ban discharge petition as of May 14. No stock-trading ban had become law in the sources reviewed. The ad's own text was not obtained, so it is not rated.

claims.claim: Turek skipped an Iowa farm-bill vote, backs California's Prop 12 and opposed a bill against labeling 'fake meat' as real (spokesman Billy Fuerst).

record.t: Iowa House vote records were not checked in this pass. The Free Beacon documented missed water-quality and veterans appropriations votes on May 1–2, 2026 (see Turek file), not a farm bill.

claims.claim: Turek 'stole from taxpayers' by taking per diem while missing votes.

record.t: A characterization. Per diem amounts were not independently checked.

said.t: Posted that Iowans 'shouldn't have to foot the bill' for the Iran war and called for an immediate end to it.

did.t: Voted against the September war-powers resolution and said another resolution wasn't needed. A Community Note on her post said she had voted four times that year against an immediate end.

said.t: Pledged to be Trump's 'strongest ally' in the Senate.

did.t: Criticized Trump's temporary lifting of beef-import tariffs and later broke with him on ending the Iran war.

note.t: From the House Clerk index, she has filed an annual report every year, each after an extension (filed in August), and one periodic transaction report, on April 5, 2021. The PDFs could not be opened. NOTUS reports her 2025 annual disclosure lists her husband's $1M–$5M interest in High Street Insurance Partners, a private-equity-backed brokerage, and that her 2021 disclosure showed him selling an interest in a private insurance company for over $1M. Democratic groups claim her net worth rose by up to $7M, 10-fold or 15-fold since she was first elected; those figures come from partisan sources and were not checked against the disclosures. In September 2026, Defend The Vote (Brian Lemek) filed a complaint with the House Office of Congressional Conduct. It alleges special access for her husband's insurance trade group and that his government-affairs role was left off her disclosure. A complaint does not open an investigation by itself; no OCC decision was reported as of 2026-10-14. She denies wrongdoing, and her campaign says her husband is not a lobbyist and has never lobbied her. She sits on the House Ethics Committee.

committees: Appropriations (Homeland Security, Financial Services, Agriculture subcommittees)

The sample used is: the official House bio (3 claims), the campaign site as quoted by Ballotpedia News, her first TV ad (May 12, 2026) as described in reporting, and her recurring debate/X claims (stock sale, wealth source, Turek's 58% absences). 9 claims, 6 of them checkable facts.

recordx.note: Every annual report from 2020–2025 was filed after an extension (e.g., the 2025 report: extension filed 2026-04-27, report filed 2026-08-13). Extensions are allowed and not a violation. No official missed-vote % was retrieved (GovTrack blocked); Newsweek, citing American Journal News, reports 33 missed floor votes and 163 committee votes since 2021. FEC notices (RFAI) were not checked (fec.gov blocked).

corp.t: Corporate and trade-association PACs have given in every cycle. Gross 2025–26 FEC committee records (through about early Oct. 2026) show about $801,500 from corporate PACs (e.g., General Dynamics, Boeing, Alliant Energy, DaVita) and $514,500 from trade PACs (e.g., the National Association of Broadcasters, Independent Insurance Agents & Brokers, auto dealers, pork producers). Earlier cycles: about $57,000 corporate plus $50,700 trade in 2020; $662,750 plus $312,685 in 2022; $631,500 plus $343,631 in 2024. AFP Action, the Koch-network super PAC, reported about $6.9M in independent expenditures supporting her. NOTUS reports InsurePAC gave more than $67,000 to her and affiliated PACs.

lobby.t: AIPAC PAC: $7,900 direct and about $22,475 in earmarks in 2022, and $10,000 direct in 2024. In 2026, a $5,000 contribution (Sept. 2, 2025) was followed by a −$5,000 entry (Sept. 8, 2025), net $0. Also U.S. Israel PAC $2,500 (2020–22) and Republican Jewish Coalition PAC $22,211 (2020–26). No United Democracy Project spending in this race in the FEC data.

research_notes: MONEY: Totals are from the FEC all-candidates summary (weball26) for S6IA00314, through 2026-06-30. 'other' ($2,714,376.17) is transfers from authorized committees, mainly her House committee (Ashley Hinson for Congress, C00706267, renamed Ashley for Iowa per FEC records). Wikipedia's race table matches the FEC totals. The business/ideological PAC split comes from FEC bulk committee-to-candidate records, which run later than June 30 and are gross (refunds netted per line), so they are reported in money_flags, not src. Itemized vs. unitemized individual giving was not available. OUTSIDE: Spending is from the FEC 2026 IE bulk file (filed through about Sept. 24), deduplicated by spender and transaction ID and keeping the latest amendment, so it understates late-September and October spending; for example, SLF's large fall buys mostly appear against Turek rather than for Hinson. The NRSC $8.76M is coordinated party spending (24C), not an IE. ISRAEL: AIPAC PAC figures are from its own FEC schedules. The 2026 −$5,000 entry is shown as filed; whether the campaign refunded it or AIPAC PAC voided it is not stated. ETHICS: The OCC complaint is an allegation by an advocacy group (Defend The Vote, which endorsed Turek in May 2026 per his campaign's news page, and whose PAC gave Turek's campaign $5,000 per FEC records), not a finding. The husband's business is his own record; it is included only because it appears on her joint disclosure and in the complaint's allegations about her office.
